SOCIAL-001.prerequisites: No special access is required beyond a standard internet connection; this is entirely passive, unauthenticated reconnaissance. Written authorization should explicitly name which employees (or 'all publicly-identifiable staff') may be profiled and state whether any follow-on phishing/vishing/physical phase may use the collected data. OSINT tooling (theHarvester, Maltego Community Edition, Sherlock, exiftool) and, if in scope, a Have I Been Pwned API key for domain-breach cross-referencing.
SOCIAL-001.whatItIs: This is about how much useful attack-planning information leaks out just from employees' public social media (LinkedIn, X, Instagram, GitHub) and the company's own public materials. No single post is a problem by itself — a job title here, a badge photo there, an out-of-office message somewhere else. But put dozens of these small details together across many employees and platforms, and an attacker can build a surprisingly detailed picture of the company, good enough to craft a very convincing pretext, without ever touching the network.
SOCIAL-001.rootCause: Nobody is actually watching for this. There's no process that defines what counts as 'sensitive when combined with other posts,' and no one is responsible for periodically searching for and flagging this kind of accumulated exposure before an attacker finds it first.
SOCIAL-001.impact: An attacker assembles an accurate email-naming-convention guess, a working org chart, and a set of highly personalized pretexts (e.g. referencing a project a specific employee posted about), which materially raises phishing and vishing success rates. Badge photos or office-interior details visible in employee posts can also directly assist physical-intrusion planning by revealing badge design, floor layout, or signage.
stepsToIdentify: Run passive reconnaissance against the organization's domain and named employees using OSINT tooling to build an initial employee list and email-format inventory.
Cross-reference employee job titles and reporting-line hints from LinkedIn against the organization's actual structure to assess how complete an org chart an outsider could reconstruct.
Search image metadata and visual backgrounds of employee-posted photos (conference badges, office selfies, whiteboards) for badge designs, internal tool UI, or asset tags.
Check breach-data aggregators for the organization's own domain to see whether employee credentials appear in historical breaches, compounding the OSINT picture with real password patterns.
Review job postings and vendor case studies for technology-stack disclosure (named security products, ticketing systems, SSO providers) that narrows pretext design.
Score the aggregate exposure — org-chart completeness, email-format certainty, named tool inventory, physical-layout clues — since the finding is about the combination, not any single item.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the rules of engagement authorize OSINT collection against named employees and explicitly define whether the output may feed a later phishing, vishing, or physical-access phase.

Compile the collected data into a structured per-employee dossier (role, manager, referenced tools, pretext-relevant personal detail) without accessing any private or authentication-gated account content.

Draft one or two sample pretext scenarios that demonstrate how the aggregated OSINT could be used, strictly as a documented illustration for the report rather than live use outside an authorized follow-on phase.
Where the statement of work includes a follow-on phishing/vishing/physical phase, hand the dossier to that phase's operators as scoped; otherwise stop at documentation.
Record which specific posts or platforms contributed the highest-value information so the report can point to fixable sources instead of a generic 'reduce your footprint' recommendation.
Do not contact, connect with, or message any employee's personal account during this phase — the activity is observation-only.

variants: Physical-security-specific OSINT: mining employee photos for badge design/colour-coding, building interior layout, or visible asset tags to inform a later tailgating or badge-cloning engagement.
Vendor/supply-chain OSINT: profiling the target's known vendors or MSPs to build a trusted-third-party impersonation pretext instead of impersonating internal staff.

Executive-specific OSINT (whaling preparation): building a travel/schedule picture of a named executive from conference speaker lists and posts to time a business-email-compromise attempt around a verifiable absence.
Continuous-monitoring variant: standing up ongoing alerts for newly indexed employee content rather than a one-time snapshot, reflecting how real adversaries maintain a living target profile.
mitigation: Publish and train staff on a concrete 'what not to post' guideline focused on aggregation risk (badge photos, whiteboards, ticket screenshots, org-chart-revealing job changes) rather than an unenforceable blanket social-media policy.

Where feasible, reduce certainty of the public email-naming convention, or accept the trade-off and compensate with stronger email authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC enforcement) instead of relying on obscurity alone.
Run periodic OSINT self-assessments and route findings back to the specific business unit generating the exposure rather than a single generic company-wide reminder.
Enforce privacy-conscious social profile defaults during onboarding, particularly for staff in security, finance, and executive-support roles.
Monitor breach-data feeds for the organization's own domain and proactively force credential resets when employee emails surface in new breach dumps.
Fold verified OSINT findings into the security-awareness and phishing-simulation program so employees see concretely how their own public information could be used against them.
Extend takedown/monitoring processes to cover employee-posted conference badges and event photos specifically, since these recur every conference season and are a repeatable, fixable source.

SOCIAL-002.prerequisites: Written authorization specifically covering live pretext calls against the help desk, naming which real (or pre-arranged decoy) accounts may be targeted, an agreed safe-word to halt a call before a real reset completes, and a point of contact who can vouch for the test if escalated. A phone/VoIP line for outbound calling and, ideally, an OSINT dossier from a prior recon phase to make the pretext credible.
SOCIAL-002.whatItIs: Help desks often reset a password or re-register MFA based only on things the caller says over the phone — employee ID, date of birth, manager's name — instead of confirming identity through a channel the caller can't fake. Since that kind of personal info is often findable online or from an old data breach, an attacker can simply call in, pretend to be the employee, and walk away with a working login — no phishing email required.
SOCIAL-002.rootCause: Identity checks for sensitive help-desk requests rely on knowledge (things you know) instead of an independent channel the attacker can't also control, like calling back a verified number. On top of that, help-desk staff are usually measured on how fast they handle calls, which pushes them to skip careful verification when a caller sounds normal and mildly urgent.
SOCIAL-002.impact: A successful reset yields a working credential — and, if MFA re-enrollment is bundled into the same call, a fresh MFA factor bound to the attacker's own device — providing initial access equivalent to a phished credential without requiring the victim to click anything. The legitimate user typically has no reason to suspect a problem until they themselves are locked out.
stepsToIdentify: Review the help desk's documented reset/re-enrollment procedure directly (the runbook or knowledge-base article), rather than relying on what agents say from memory.
Assess whether the verification data points the procedure requires (employee ID, manager name, department, DOB) are independently discoverable via OSINT or public breach data.

Determine whether the flow includes any out-of-band confirmation — a callback to a number already on file, a notification to the user's manager, a push to a previously enrolled device — that an attacker couldn't also intercept.
Check whether MFA re-enrollment is bundled into the same call as a password reset, since that is a materially higher-risk action than a password reset alone.
With client permission, review a sample of recent reset tickets for prior instances where verification was skipped, rushed, or escalated under caller pressure.
Compare the IT help desk's process against any parallel channel (HR, facilities) handling similar 'locked out' requests, since the weakest channel sets the organization's real exposure.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the statement of work explicitly authorizes live pretext calls, defines in-scope accounts (real or pre-arranged decoy), and sets a hard stop the instant a genuine reset would complete.
Build the call pretext from previously-authorized OSINT and identify likely verification questions based on the documented procedure reviewed during discovery.
Place the call using a plausible internal-caller persona under mild time pressure, and record whether the agent follows, skips, or shortcuts the required verification steps.

If verification is bypassed and a reset is offered, disclose the test per the pre-agreed stop condition immediately rather than completing it, unless the SOW specifically authorizes completing a reset against a pre-arranged decoy account.
Flag any case where MFA re-enrollment is also offered in the same call as a separate, higher-severity finding, since it represents full account takeover rather than a password reset alone.
Repeat with two to three independent calls across different agents, times of day, and urgency framings to distinguish an individual lapse from a systemic procedural gap.
Debrief each involved agent supportively and promptly after the call, making clear the test evaluates the process rather than the individual.

variants: Vishing the employee's manager instead of the help desk, requesting an 'emergency' access grant on the employee's behalf.
Chained pretext: calling HR first to confirm employment status or start date, then using that confirmation as a credibility signal in the subsequent IT call.
Text/chat-based pretexting via an internal Slack/Teams help-desk channel, where identity verification may be weaker than the phone process.
SIM-swap-adjacent variant testing whether the help desk would action a registered phone-number change for MFA SMS delivery under the same weak verification.
mitigation: Require a verification factor the impersonator cannot also supply — a callback to the number already on file in HR systems, not the number the caller is currently using.
Separate password reset from MFA re-enrollment procedurally; require a stronger, manager-notified process specifically for re-enrolling MFA or changing a registered device or phone number.
Route any request framed with urgency or emotional pressure through a mandatory second-approver step regardless of how convincing the caller sounds.

Train help-desk staff specifically on pretexting patterns — manufactured urgency, minor plausible confusion about their own details, authority-adjacent name-dropping — rather than generic awareness content.
Log and periodically audit a sample of reset calls against the documented procedure, with findings routed to help-desk management rather than treated as isolated incidents.

Consider self-service identity-proofing (push notification to a previously enrolled device, or a verified identity-proofing flow) that removes the human judgment call for the riskiest actions entirely.
Recognize and reward agents who correctly refuse or escalate a suspicious request, rather than measuring only average call-handling time.

SOCIAL-003.prerequisites: Written authorization naming the specific facility/floor in scope, an escort or point of contact who can vouch for the assessor if security or staff intervene, and a pre-agreed identification method (assessment ID card, letter of authorization) to present if challenged. A visitor badge or cover pretext consistent with the SOW, and a camera/notebook for evidence capture.
SOCIAL-003.whatItIs: This looks at the physical security protecting a server room or data closet as a whole system, not just one door — where the badge readers are, whether there's a mantrap or anti-passback logic, whether visitors actually sign in and get escorted, whether alarms and cameras cover the right spots, and how fast anyone actually notices a door propped open or forced.
SOCIAL-003.rootCause: Physical access control usually gets designed once, during the original construction, and is never re-checked against how the space is actually used day to day. Each individual piece — a badge reader, a door alarm, a camera — can look fine on its own, while the system as a whole still lets an unbadged person walk up to sensitive equipment, because nobody owns testing the whole chain end to end.
SOCIAL-003.impact: Physical access to a server room bypasses essentially every network-layer control — an intruder can attach a rogue device to the switch, image a drive directly, install a hardware keylogger, or simply remove equipment, and physical compromise is far harder to detect after the fact than a network intrusion since it often leaves no log trail at all.
stepsToIdentify: Walk the facility's public and semi-public areas to map every path that could reach the server room, including secondary/emergency doors, loading docks, and shared-tenant corridors in multi-tenant buildings.

Observe badge reader type and placement at each entry point (proximity vs. multi-factor, single door vs. mantrap) and note any door propped open for delivery or smoking-break convenience during the observation window.
Review visitor sign-in and escort policy against actual practice by observing whether visitors are consistently escorted past the point they'd need to be to reach the server room.
Check alarm response: note whether a propped-open or forced door triggers a visible/audible alert and, if possible, how long it takes for staff to investigate.
Assess camera coverage and retention for the approach corridors and the server room door itself, not just the room's interior.

Review whether server room access logs are actually reconciled against the current employee/vendor list, or whether stale access grants (departed employees, expired vendor contracts) persist unnoticed.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the SOW authorizes physical-access testing at this specific site, defines the safe-word/ID-presentation procedure if challenged by staff or security, and lists an emergency contact reachable during the test window.

Attempt to reach the server room's outer perimeter using only publicly available access (front desk, unlocked secondary doors) without presenting any credential, and stop at the first door requiring genuine authentication if no weakness is found.

Where a weakness is found (propped door, unattended visitor sign-in, tailgating opportunity), proceed only as far as needed to demonstrate reach to the server room door itself; do not enter the room or touch equipment unless the SOW explicitly authorizes it.

If challenged by staff, immediately present the pre-agreed authorization method and stand down rather than attempting to argue past a suspicious employee — a correctly suspicious employee is a passing result for the organization, not a test failure.
Photograph (per SOW terms) the specific control gap exploited — the propped door, the unmonitored corridor, the missing escort — as evidence for the report.
Note the elapsed time from initial building entry to reaching the server room door, since dwell time is itself a meaningful metric for the client's incident-response planning.

variants: Shared-tenant/multi-occupancy building variant, where the server room sits behind the target's own door but the building's shared corridors and loading dock are outside the target's direct control.
After-hours variant testing whether reduced staffing changes challenge behavior and alarm-response times compared to business hours.
Vendor/contractor-impersonation variant (HVAC, cabling, cleaning) testing whether a plausible service uniform and clipboard substitute for genuine authorization.
Colocation/data-center-cage variant, where the finding concerns whether the facility's own controls prevent other tenants from reaching the target's specific cage.
mitigation: Treat server-room physical access as a single end-to-end system with one accountable owner, rather than a set of independently-managed controls (badge system, alarm system, visitor policy) that are never tested together.
Enforce mantrap or anti-passback logic at the server-room boundary specifically, even where the wider building uses simple proximity badges.
Alarm every server-room door for prop-open and forced-entry conditions, and route the alert to a monitored channel with a defined, tested response SLA.
Enforce and periodically audit visitor escort policy with unannounced spot checks rather than relying on policy documentation alone.
Reconcile server-room access grants against current HR/vendor-contract status on a fixed schedule, removing stale access automatically where the identity system supports it.
Extend camera coverage and adequate retention to approach corridors, not just the server-room interior, so an incident's full path can be reconstructed.
Run this assessment periodically (at minimum annually, and after any facility layout change) rather than treating a single physical pentest as a one-time validation.

SOCIAL-004.prerequisites: Written authorization explicitly covering RFID capture and duplication (this involves handling employees' physical credentials or their signals and needs its own explicit line in the SOW, separate from general physical-testing authorization). An RFID read/write tool (Proxmark3 or Flipper Zero) and, for MIFARE Classic assessment, mfoc/mfcuk or libnfc. Physical proximity to badge readers or badge-carrying employees within the card's normal read range.
SOCIAL-004.whatItIs: A lot of organizations still use old 125kHz proximity cards (like HID Prox) that just broadcast a fixed, unencrypted ID number with zero verification — or 13.56MHz MIFARE Classic cards, whose encryption was cracked years ago. Either way, someone standing a few centimeters away (or further, with a stronger antenna) can read your card's ID and write an identical copy onto a blank card.
SOCIAL-004.rootCause: 125kHz proximity cards have no authentication at all — the reader just trusts any device that sends a valid-looking ID number, so 'security' here really just means the number is hard to guess, not hard to copy. MIFARE Classic does have an authentication scheme, but its encryption is broken badly enough that recovering the keys and cloning the card is practical with cheap, widely available tools. Newer card types (DESFire EV2/EV3, iCLASS SE) use modern, unbroken encryption and aren't practically cloneable the same way.
SOCIAL-004.impact: A cloned badge grants the same physical access as the original without the legitimate holder's knowledge, defeating every downstream physical control (server room, executive floor, data center cage) that relies on that badge for authorization, and because the clone is a working duplicate rather than a stolen physical object, the legitimate employee has no reason to report a lost card.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the card technology in use by passive RF fingerprinting (frequency band and modulation) from an authorized vantage point, without attempting to read any specific employee's card content yet.

Confirm whether the deployed system is 125kHz proximity (inherently cloneable, no crypto), MIFARE Classic (crypto broken, cloneable with moderate effort), or a modern DESFire/iCLASS SE deployment (not practically cloneable with commodity tools).

Where MIFARE Classic is suspected, attempt a nested/dark-side key-recovery attack against a test card provided by the client (never an employee's live card without explicit written consent) to confirm exploitability rather than assuming it from the chip family alone.

Assess achievable read range with the assessment hardware (both close-proximity and any longer-range antenna in scope) to characterize realistic attack distance in a crowded area (elevator, cafe, transit).

Check whether the same card is also used for logical-access or payment functions (badge doubling as building access and cafeteria payment, for example), since a clone would then also carry that additional value.
Review whether any secondary factor (PIN pad, security-guard visual check) supplements the badge at the highest-sensitivity doors, which would reduce the real-world impact of a successful clone.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the SOW's explicit, separate authorization for RFID capture/duplication and clarify whether testing must use client-provided test cards only or may (with specific consent) attempt a live employee's card in a controlled, observed setting.
Using client-provided test cards, capture the card's UID and, for MIFARE Classic, recover sector keys using a nested/dark-side attack.
Write the captured data to blank card stock (or a Flipper Zero/Proxmark3 emulation mode) and verify the clone is accepted by a test reader before attempting it against a live production door.
Where authorized to test against a live door, present the clone at a low-sensitivity door first to confirm functional equivalence before any higher-sensitivity door is attempted.

Document the elapsed time from initial card proximity to a working clone, since this is the realistic figure a client needs for risk-acceptance decisions (e.g. is a few seconds of elevator proximity enough).
Do not retain cloned credential data beyond the engagement; securely wipe cloned physical cards and any captured key material at test completion and note this in the report.

variants: Long-range relay/amplifier variant, testing achievable read distance beyond casual pocket proximity to assess crowded-space risk (elevators, transit, conference badges).
Combined badge-and-payment clone, where the same physical card is used for both facility access and an internal cashless payment system.

Signal-relay attack variant (relaying a live card's response in real time between two colluding devices) rather than a stored-and-replayed static clone, relevant primarily to higher-frequency systems with weak anti-relay timing.
Vendor/loaner-badge variant testing whether temporary contractor badges use weaker (often 125kHz legacy) technology than full-time employee badges.
mitigation: Migrate from 125kHz proximity and MIFARE Classic to a modern, mutually-authenticated credential technology (DESFire EV2/EV3, iCLASS SE) that has no practical cloning attack with commodity tools.
Where legacy readers cannot be replaced immediately, add a second factor (PIN, biometric, or security-guard visual check) at the highest-sensitivity doors so a cloned badge alone is insufficient.
Disable or physically shield unused/backup readers that still accept the legacy technology, since a single legacy fallback reader undermines an otherwise-upgraded system.
Monitor for anomalous badge-use patterns (same badge used at geographically implausible doors within a short window) as a compensating detective control during migration.
Reduce achievable read range where feasible (reader placement, shielding) and educate staff on RF-proximity risk in crowded public spaces.
Ensure temporary/contractor/loaner badge stock is provisioned on the same secure technology as full-time employee badges rather than a cheaper legacy fallback.
Include badge-technology review in any facility security assessment cadence, since legacy readers are frequently discovered years after a supposedly-complete access-control upgrade.

SOCIAL-005.prerequisites: Written authorization naming the specific locations/events where QR codes may be placed (lobby, parking validation signage, conference booth) and confirming they will be removed at test conclusion. A QR-generation tool, a controlled landing page under a domain the assessor owns, and click/scan analytics to measure engagement without capturing anything beyond what the SOW authorizes.
SOCIAL-005.whatItIs: This attack puts a QR code somewhere an employee would naturally scan it without thinking twice — a fake parking-validation sticker, a 'scan for the WiFi password' table sign, a flyer stuck over a real poster. It works because a QR code doesn't visually show where it leads, so the normal 'let me check this link before I click it' instinct never kicks in the way it would for a suspicious URL.
SOCIAL-005.rootCause: QR codes are designed to hide their destination — you can't tell where one goes just by looking at it, and most phone cameras only show a small, easy-to-miss preview of the actual link before opening it. So the habit people have built up for spotting a shady link in an email simply doesn't transfer to a scanned code.
SOCIAL-005.impact: A scanned malicious code can redirect to a credential-harvesting login clone, prompt installation of a malicious mobile profile/app, or simply confirm the target is a receptive victim for a follow-on vishing or phishing attempt — and because scanning happens on a personal or lightly-managed mobile device, it often falls outside the visibility of corporate email/web security controls entirely.
stepsToIdentify: Survey existing legitimate QR code usage across the facility (parking, menus, event signage, badge check-in) to understand what a plausible fake would need to visually match.
Assess whether any organizational guidance or training addresses QR-specific caution, distinct from general phishing-link awareness.

Check whether the corporate mobile device management (MDM) policy, where devices are managed, would flag or block a known-malicious destination reached via QR scan the same way it would a clicked email link.
Review physical locations with high foot traffic and low staff oversight (lobby, elevator lobby, break room bulletin board) as realistic placement points for a test code.
Confirm with the client whether the test population's devices are BYOD or corporate-managed, since this materially changes both realistic risk and what telemetry will be available afterward.
Identify a baseline scan-rate expectation (e.g. from prior awareness testing) to contextualize the result rather than reporting a raw scan count without benchmark.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the SOW names the exact placement locations, the takedown time, and the landing-page behavior (informational disclosure page vs. simulated credential-harvest form) authorized for the test.
Generate a QR code pointing to an assessor-controlled landing page hosted on a domain that does not impersonate any real, named vendor or brand used by the organization.
Place the code in the authorized location, visually consistent with legitimate signage nearby, for the agreed duration only.
Log scan events (timestamp, approximate location if multiple codes are used, device user-agent) without collecting any personal data beyond what the SOW authorizes.
Where the landing page includes a simulated credential form, immediately disclose the test to anyone who submits data and do not store the submitted values beyond a pass/fail count.
Remove all physical codes at the agreed end time regardless of results, and confirm removal with photographic evidence for the report.

variants: Parking-validation or 'scan to pay' overlay sticker placed on a legitimate payment or validation kiosk.
Conference/event badge-swap variant, where the code is on a fake sponsor flyer inside a real event.

Malicious mobile configuration-profile variant (iOS/Android) testing whether the landing page could prompt a profile install rather than just a web redirect — assessed at the disclosure/consent level only, not deployed against real devices without explicit separate authorization.
Combined bait variant pairing the QR code with a physical item (a USB drive, a branded pen) to test whether visual/physical plausibility compounds the effect.
mitigation: Extend phishing-awareness training to explicitly cover QR codes, since the 'inspect the link before clicking' habit does not transfer automatically to a scanned code.
Encourage or provision phone camera/QR-scanner apps that show the full resolved URL prominently before navigating, rather than a small, easily-missed preview.
Apply mobile threat defense or DNS-filtering coverage to corporate-managed devices so a malicious QR destination is blocked the same way a malicious email link would be.
Establish a physical-signage integrity process (periodic walk-throughs checking for overlay stickers or unauthorized flyers) for high-traffic areas.

Where the organization uses QR codes for legitimate purposes (parking, menus, check-in), apply a consistent visual standard (branded frame, verified-source watermark) that makes an unofficial overlay easier to spot.
Include QR-based pretexts in the ongoing phishing-simulation program rather than treating email as the only simulated channel.
Provide a simple, well-publicized reporting path for 'suspicious sign/code' the same way phishing-email reporting is publicized.

SOCIAL-006.prerequisites: Written authorization specifically covering examination of the organization's discarded materials (this is legally sensitive in some jurisdictions and must be scoped precisely — waste on the organization's own premises/dumpsters, not a third-party waste hauler's property, unless separately cleared). Gloves, a flashlight, and a way to photograph findings in place before returning materials undisturbed.
SOCIAL-006.whatItIs: This checks whether sensitive material — printed passwords, org charts, network diagrams, unshredded financial documents, old hard drives or backup tapes — can be found in the company's trash or recycling before it's collected. It's a gap in how documents and old equipment get disposed of, not a digital vulnerability.
SOCIAL-006.rootCause: A document-destruction policy exists on paper, but it isn't actually followed at the point where someone throws something away — shredders are often slow, inconvenient, or far from where people work, so staff just use the regular trash bin instead. Old computers and drives sometimes skip the official wipe/destroy process entirely if they're handled outside IT's normal process for retiring equipment.
SOCIAL-006.impact: Recovered material can directly supply a follow-on pretext (an org chart, a vendor invoice with real account details, a temporary password on a sticky note) or, in the case of improperly wiped drives/media, expose the underlying data directly without any exploitation effort at all.
stepsToIdentify: Identify all disposal points in scope — interior bins, exterior dumpsters, recycling containers, and any e-waste/hardware-retirement staging area — and confirm which are accessible without trespass beyond what the SOW authorizes.
Observe the collection schedule to time the assessment shortly before pickup, maximizing the realistic volume of material available without needing to disturb a freshly-emptied container.
Note whether shredding bins/services are present and whether their placement (e.g. one shredder for an entire floor) plausibly explains any observed non-compliance.
Check whether any decommissioned hardware (drives, backup tapes, printed reports) appears in general disposal rather than the organization's IT asset-retirement stream.
Cross-reference any names, account numbers, or system details found against the OSINT dossier from a prior phase to assess how much this source adds beyond what's already public.
Document material in place with photographs before determining what, if anything, will be retained as evidence per the SOW's evidence-handling terms.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the SOW authorizes examination of the specific disposal points identified, and clarify evidence-handling rules (photograph in place vs. retain a sample) before touching anything.
Examine accessible waste without trespassing beyond the authorized property line or disturbing locked/enclosed containers not covered by the authorization.
Photograph any sensitive material found in place, redacting or handling live credentials/PII per the SOW's data-handling terms rather than transcribing full values into the working notes.
Return all material to its original location undisturbed once documentation is complete, unless the SOW specifically authorizes retaining a sample as evidence.

Classify each finding by realistic sensitivity (a discarded lunch menu vs. an unshredded W-2) rather than reporting raw item counts, since volume without severity context is not actionable for the client.
Note the specific source point (which bin, which floor) for each finding so remediation can be targeted rather than facility-wide.

examplePayloads.command: Tier: low (generic marketing material) / medium (internal org chart, non-sensitive memo) / high (credentials, financial records, unwiped media).

variants: E-waste/hardware variant specifically targeting a decommissioned-equipment staging area rather than general office trash.
Off-site records-storage variant, assessing a third-party document storage/shredding vendor's own handling chain rather than the client's on-premise disposal.
Remote/home-office variant assessing whether remote employees follow the same document-destruction standard the office enforces.
Timing-based variant comparing findings immediately before vs. immediately after a scheduled collection, to characterize how disposal volume/sensitivity fluctuates.
mitigation: Place cross-cut shredders (or secure locked shred-collection bins serviced by a certified vendor) at the point of use, not centrally, so the convenient option is also the secure one.
Route all decommissioned hardware through a single, audited IT asset-retirement process with certified data destruction, and reconcile disposed-hardware serial numbers against that log periodically.

Extend document-handling policy explicitly to remote/home-office staff, with a defined process (mail-back shredding service, provided personal shredder) rather than assuming office practice transfers.
Audit disposal points periodically (unannounced, similar to this assessment) rather than relying on policy documentation alone to confirm compliance.
Contractually require any third-party shredding/records-storage vendor to provide certificates of destruction and periodically audit their own chain of custody.
Include document-disposal hygiene in new-hire and periodic security-awareness training with concrete, facility-specific guidance rather than generic 'shred sensitive documents' language.

Consider transitioning frequently-discarded sensitive artifacts (temporary password slips, printed reports) to a digital-only or time-limited-display format to reduce what's disposed of physically at all.

SOCIAL-007.prerequisites: Written authorization specifically covering live impersonation of internal IT support and any resulting request to install or accept remote-access software, plus a hard stop condition before any real remote-access session is established against a production endpoint (or explicit authorization to proceed against a pre-arranged decoy machine). A phone/VoIP line and, ideally, OSINT identifying the organization's actual IT support naming conventions and ticketing tools.
SOCIAL-007.whatItIs: The tester calls, messages, or files a fake ticket pretending to be internal IT support, and tries to convince an employee to install remote-access software (like AnyDesk or TeamViewer) or accept an unexpected remote session. If a real attacker pulled this off, they'd get full, interactive control of that computer.
SOCIAL-007.rootCause: Employees are trained to respond quickly and helpfully to IT requests, and they have no reliable way to check whether a caller claiming to be internal IT actually is — especially when the caller mentions something plausible and mildly urgent, like a pending update or a 'flagged' account. There's usually no standard habit of calling back through a verified number or checking a ticket number before handing over remote access.
SOCIAL-007.impact: A successful session grants the same level of control a legitimate remote-support session would — full desktop access, file transfer, and often local administrative rights — making this one of the highest-impact social engineering outcomes tested, comparable to a successful malware execution via phishing but achieved through voice/chat persuasion alone.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm what remote-access tools the organization's actual IT support uses and whether that tool is allow-listed/blocked for anything else, since a pretext using an unexpected tool is easier for a suspicious employee to catch.
Assess whether employees have any established way to verify an IT contact's legitimacy (a callback number, a ticket-number lookup, a known internal chat channel) before granting remote access.
Review whether local administrative rights are broadly available to standard users, since this changes the ceiling of what a successful session could achieve.
Check whether endpoint protection would flag or block execution of an unexpected remote-access tool even if the user is persuaded to run it.

Determine whether the organization's real IT support ever legitimately cold-contacts users (rather than only responding to user-initiated tickets), since if it doesn't, any inbound 'IT support' contact is itself a red flag employees should be trained to recognize.
Identify a representative sample of employees/departments for testing rather than a single individual, to assess whether susceptibility varies meaningfully by team or seniority.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the SOW's explicit authorization for this specific technique, the hard stop before a real session on a production endpoint, and (if applicable) the pre-arranged decoy machine to use instead.
Build the pretext using previously-authorized OSINT and knowledge of the organization's real IT naming conventions, ticketing system, and typical remote-access tooling.
Initiate contact (call, chat, or fabricated ticket) with a plausible, moderately urgent technical framing, and record whether the employee asks any verifying question before proceeding.

If the employee agrees to install or open a remote-access tool, guide them only as far as confirming the tool is running and would accept a connection, then disclose the test immediately rather than establishing an actual session against a live production machine.
Where a pre-arranged decoy machine is in scope, proceed to establish the session and demonstrate (without further action) that control was achieved, then disconnect and disclose.
Note precisely which verification step, if any, the employee attempted and at what point in the interaction, since this is more actionable for training than a simple pass/fail.
Debrief the employee supportively and immediately, emphasizing this evaluates the organization's process, not the individual's judgment.

examplePayloads.command: Confirm remote-access tool (AnyDesk/TeamViewer) shows an active incoming-connection prompt or established session ID; do not proceed to file access, credential capture, or persistence.

examplePayloads.command: Verify the fabricated ticket number format matches the organization's real ITSM numbering convention observed during discovery, to make the test realistic rather than artificially easy or hard.

examplePayloads.command: Confirm whether EDR/AV on the decoy endpoint generates any alert on execution of the remote-access installer, independent of whether the human interaction succeeded.

examplePayloads.command: Record: department, contact method, pretext used, verification attempted (Y/N and what), outcome, time-to-compliance.

variants: Chat-based variant via the organization's internal messaging platform (Slack/Teams) rather than a phone call, testing a different trust channel.
Fabricated-ticket variant where the employee is told to click a link in a ticket-notification email rather than being asked directly during a live call.
Executive-assistant variant targeting support staff who manage a senior executive's device, since compromise there often yields broader access.

Persistent-access variant (decoy machine only) demonstrating whether the tester could additionally establish a persistence mechanism during the authorized session, relevant to assessing full attack-chain impact rather than initial access alone.
mitigation: Establish and train staff on a mandatory callback-verification habit before granting any remote-access request, using a number looked up independently rather than one provided by the caller.

Have real IT support operate on a ticket-driven, user-initiated model wherever possible, and explicitly train staff that unsolicited 'IT is calling you' contact is unusual and should be verified before any action.
Allow-list only the organization's sanctioned remote-access tool at the endpoint level, so an unexpected tool cannot even launch regardless of the human decision.
Restrict local administrative rights on standard endpoints so a successful session's ceiling is lower even if the social-engineering step succeeds.
Ensure EDR/AV policy flags execution of common remote-access tools outside of IT's expected usage window or device group.

Fold this specific pretext (impersonated IT support requesting remote access) explicitly into the security-awareness and phishing-simulation program, since it is measurably distinct from email-based phishing.
Recognize and positively reinforce employees who correctly verify before granting access, to counter the instinct that questioning IT is itself unhelpful or risky.

SOCIAL-008.prerequisites: Written authorization defining the target population, the specific pretext theme(s) approved for use, what constitutes a 'compliance' event (link click vs. credential entry vs. attachment execution), and explicit sign-off that no real credential harvesting will retain submitted values. A phishing-simulation platform (GoPhish, King Phisher, or a commercial equivalent), a sending domain that will not permanently damage the organization's own domain reputation, and coordination with the mail security team to avoid unrelated incident-response activity being triggered.
SOCIAL-008.whatItIs: A controlled, authorized phishing campaign sent to some or all employees to measure, realistically, how many people click the link, how many enter their credentials, and how many report it — against a specific pretext. This gives the organization a baseline number to track over time and figure out where training is actually needed.
SOCIAL-008.rootCause: Email gives a busy employee very few quick, reliable clues to tell a well-made fake from the real thing — the sender's display name is trivial to fake, lookalike domains are cheap to register, and the urgent, authoritative tone of a good phishing email is specifically written to stop someone from pausing to think.
SOCIAL-008.impact: A real-world equivalent of a successful campaign delivers credential harvest at scale or an initial malware foothold via attachment/link, and the simulation's measured click and submission rates give the organization a concrete, trackable baseline of how many real incidents a similarly-crafted live campaign would likely produce.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm with the client which pretext themes are in scope (IT/password reset, HR/benefits, shipping notification, executive request) and which are explicitly excluded (no genuine crisis, medical, or emotionally exploitative themes).

Review existing email security controls (SPF/DKIM/DMARC enforcement, link rewriting/sandboxing, attachment detonation) to understand what a real attacker would need to bypass, and note where the simulation should test the human layer specifically vs. where it would just be caught by the gateway regardless.
Identify the target population and any segmentation needed (department, seniority, prior-training-completion status) for meaningful post-campaign analysis.
Confirm the organization's phishing-report mechanism (a report button, a forwarding address) is functioning and measure baseline report volume for context.
Check whether the mail security/SOC team needs advance, confidential notice to avoid the simulation triggering an unrelated real incident-response process.

Establish the specific metrics to be measured (open rate, click rate, credential-submission rate, attachment-execution rate, report rate) before launch so success isn't redefined after seeing results.
exploitationSteps: Confirm final SOW sign-off on pretext content, target list, and the credential-handling rule (no real values retained beyond a submission count) before any send.

Configure the simulation platform's sending profile, landing page, and tracking parameters, and send a small internal test batch to the assessor's own addresses to confirm rendering and tracking work correctly.
Launch the campaign to the authorized target list at the agreed time, avoiding sending during a period that could plausibly be confused with a real ongoing incident.
Monitor delivery and engagement in near-real-time so any unexpected side effect (help-desk flood, unintended forwarding to non-scoped recipients) can be caught early.

Where an employee submits simulated credentials, immediately serve a clear 'this was a test' disclosure page rather than a realistic-looking success page, and do not store the submitted value beyond a yes/no flag.
Close the campaign at the agreed time, disable the landing page, and compile results segmented as agreed for the report.
Coordinate any immediate just-in-time training nudge to employees who clicked/submitted, consistent with the client's existing awareness-program design.

variants: Attachment-based variant (macro-enabled document or a benign 'canary' file that phones home on open) rather than a credential-harvesting link, to measure attachment-execution behavior specifically.

Spearphishing variant targeting a small, specifically-researched group (finance, executive assistants) with a highly tailored pretext built from the OSINT phase, rather than a broad, generic campaign.
Reply-chain/thread-hijack variant testing susceptibility to a message that appears to continue an existing plausible conversation thread.
Multi-wave variant sending an increasingly well-crafted pretext across several rounds to measure whether awareness improves (or fatigue sets in) over the assessment period.
mitigation: Enforce SPF, DKIM, and DMARC with a reject/quarantine policy to reduce trivial display-name and domain spoofing before it ever reaches an inbox.
Deploy link rewriting/sandboxing and attachment detonation at the mail gateway so a meaningful share of attempts are caught before the human layer is ever tested.
Run phishing simulations on a recurring cadence with rotating pretexts and themes, rather than a single annual test, so results reflect current susceptibility rather than a stale baseline.
Route just-in-time, contextual micro-training to employees who click or submit, rather than only an annual, generic awareness module.

Make the report-phishing mechanism a single click available directly in the mail client, and publicly track and recognize the organization's report rate as a positive metric, not just click rate as a negative one.
Segment analysis by department/role and target additional training at groups with disproportionate susceptibility rather than a one-size-fits-all program.
Coordinate simulation timing and pretext themes with the SOC/help-desk in advance to avoid wasting real incident-response effort on a known test.

SOCIAL-009.prerequisites: Written authorization naming the specific entry points in scope, a pre-agreed identification method and stop condition if challenged, and an emergency point of contact. A plausible cover item consistent with the SOW (a box, a coffee cup, a laptop bag) and, unlike SOCIAL-003's architecture review, no need for badge/reader technical access — this test targets human behavior at the door, not the access-control system design.
SOCIAL-009.whatItIs: Tailgating (also called piggybacking) means following an authorized person through a badge-controlled door without swiping your own badge — relying on the fact that most people feel awkward challenging a stranger, or hold a door open as a simple courtesy, or assume someone carrying boxes shouldn't have to stop and badge in.
SOCIAL-009.rootCause: Holding a door for someone is a normal, socially rewarded courtesy, and employees usually don't have a simple, low-awkwardness way to challenge someone who looks like they belong (business clothes, a laptop bag, walking confidently) — everyone assumes someone else will handle it if something seems off. The badge reader itself is only as strong as the human behavior around it, and that behavior undermines it completely.
SOCIAL-009.impact: A successful tailgate bypasses the badge system entirely, granting the same physical reach as a genuine badge holder without leaving an access-log entry tied to the actual person who entered, which is precisely why this often has higher real-world impact than the badge-cloning finding: it requires no technical tooling at all and leaves no electronic trace to investigate afterward.
stepsToIdentify: Observe each badge-controlled entry point during peak ingress periods (shift start, post-lunch) to characterize typical door-holding behavior and queue density.
Note whether any physical control beyond the badge reader exists to counter tailgating specifically — a mantrap, a turnstile, or a staffed security desk with a visual headcount check.
Assess whether carrying a visually plausible prop (boxes, coffee, a phone to the ear) measurably changes whether employees hold the door, based on prior awareness-test data or direct observation.

Review whether employees receive any specific tailgating-challenge training, distinct from general security-awareness content, and whether they're empowered (and psychologically supported) to challenge a stranger.
Check whether badge-in counts are reconciled against occupancy or camera-based headcounts at any point, which would surface tailgating even without catching it live.

Identify secondary/less-trafficked entry points where a lone employee holding the door might occur without any bystander at all, since these often present a materially easier target than the main entrance.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the SOW's authorized entry points, stop condition if challenged, and identification method to present immediately if stopped by staff or security.
Approach the target entry point during an observed high-traffic window carrying a plausible prop, and follow an authorized employee through without presenting a credential.
If the employee holds the door without hesitation, proceed only as far as the SOW authorizes (reaching a defined checkpoint) rather than continuing deeper into the facility unnecessarily.

If challenged at any point, immediately present the pre-agreed authorization and stand down — this is a passing result for the organization and should be logged as such, not treated as a failed test attempt.

Note the specific behavioral factor that enabled entry (prop plausibility, queue density, time of day, whether the employee made eye contact) since this is more actionable for training than a simple success/failure count.
Repeat across two to three entry points and time windows to distinguish an isolated lapse from a systemic pattern, without oversaturating any single employee's exposure to the test.

variants: Delivery/vendor-impersonation variant carrying a branded uniform or package consistent with a known, expected vendor.
Reverse-tailgating variant where the tester holds the door open for others (positioning as the 'helpful' one) to see whether staff then follow the tester's lead unquestioningly.
After-hours/reduced-staffing variant testing whether tailgating success changes meaningfully outside peak hours.
Multi-door chained variant testing whether a single successful tailgate at the perimeter also grants passage through interior badge-controlled doors without further challenge.
mitigation: Install mantraps, turnstiles, or a staffed visual-verification point at the highest-sensitivity entries, since these remove the reliance on individual employee challenge behavior entirely.
Train and psychologically empower staff with a simple, low-friction challenge script ('happy to hold the door once you've badged in') that doesn't require confrontation.
Reconcile badge-in counts against camera-based headcounts or turnstile counts periodically to surface tailgating even where it isn't caught live.
Reduce queue-density pressure at peak ingress times (additional readers, staggered shift starts) since crowding is a measurable contributor to door-holding behavior.
Include tailgating-specific scenarios in security-awareness training, distinct from generic 'be alert' messaging, with realistic prop and pretext examples.
Recognize and positively reinforce employees who correctly challenge a tailgater, to counter any perceived social cost of doing so.
Extend the same controls and training consistently to secondary/less-trafficked entrances, which this assessment often finds are weaker than the main entrance.

SOCIAL-010.prerequisites: Written authorization defining the target phone-number list (typically corporate mobile numbers, sourced from the client, not scraped independently), the approved pretext theme, and confirmation the campaign complies with applicable telecom/anti-spam regulations for the jurisdiction (e.g. TCPA-equivalent rules) since SMS carries different legal considerations than email. An SMS gateway/sending platform (Twilio or equivalent) and an assessor-controlled landing domain.
SOCIAL-010.whatItIs: A controlled test sending SMS text messages to see whether employees click a link or reply to a message pretending to be from IT, HR, a delivery company, or something similarly believable. Text messages generally get far less spam filtering than corporate email, and people often read them on a personal phone that IT barely manages, if at all.
SOCIAL-010.rootCause: SMS has nothing like email's sender-verification systems (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) — the sender name is easy to fake or spoof, phones usually show only a truncated link with little or no preview, and most employees have received far less security training and tooling for their phone's messaging app than for their work email.
SOCIAL-010.impact: A successful smish can drive the same credential-harvest or malicious-app-install outcomes as email phishing but often bypasses the corporate security stack entirely, since messages arrive over the cellular network rather than through any monitored gateway, and personal devices frequently used for this channel add another layer of reduced visibility for the security team.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the source and scope of the phone-number list to be used (client-provided corporate directory only, not independently scraped or purchased data).
Review whether the organization's mobile device management (MDM) or mobile threat defense tooling, where deployed, would flag a known-malicious SMS link.
Assess whether employees have received any training specific to SMS-based phishing, distinct from email-phishing awareness.
Check local telecom/anti-spam regulatory requirements for the jurisdiction before finalizing send volume and content, since SMS carries distinct compliance obligations from email.
Identify whether corporate numbers are BYOD or company-issued, since this affects both realistic risk and available telemetry.
Establish success metrics (click rate, response rate, reported-to-security rate) before launch, consistent with the email-phishing simulation's measurement approach.
exploitationSteps: Confirm final SOW sign-off on the number list source, pretext content, and regulatory compliance check before any send.
Configure the SMS gateway and assessor-controlled landing page, and send a small internal test batch to confirm delivery and tracking work as expected.
Launch the campaign to the authorized number list at the agreed time, avoiding any period that could be confused with a real ongoing incident.
Monitor delivery and click-through in near-real-time to catch any unexpected side effect early.
Serve a clear test-disclosure page on any click or response, and do not retain any personal data beyond a yes/no engagement flag.
Close the campaign at the agreed time, disable the landing page, and compile results for the report.

variants: Delivery-notification pretext impersonating a generic shipping carrier rather than an internal system.
Multi-factor-authentication (MFA) fatigue-adjacent variant testing response to a fake 'verify this login' SMS rather than a link-click pretext.
Two-stage variant where the SMS drives the target to call a number (vishing hand-off) rather than click a link.
Executive/high-value-target variant using a small, specifically researched number list rather than a broad campaign.
mitigation: Deploy mobile threat defense on corporate-managed devices capable of flagging known-malicious SMS links, mirroring email-gateway protection.
Extend security-awareness training explicitly to cover SMS-based phishing as a distinct channel from email.
Publicize a simple reporting path for suspicious text messages (a forwarding shortcode or a documented process) similar to the email report-phishing button.
Where feasible, favor authenticated in-app notifications over plain SMS for sensitive prompts (password reset, MFA approval) so users have a consistent, harder-to-spoof channel to trust.
Run SMS-based simulations on a recurring basis alongside email simulations, since susceptibility and awareness levels for the two channels do not necessarily track together.
Ensure any organizational legitimate use of SMS for employee communication follows a consistent, recognizable format, making an off-pattern message easier for employees to flag.

SOCIAL-011.prerequisites: Written authorization covering direct observation of employees in open work areas, common spaces, and public-facing transit (elevators, cafes near the office) if in scope. No special tooling required beyond discreet observation and note-taking; a zoom-capable camera may be used only if the SOW explicitly authorizes photographic evidence of screens/keypads.
SOCIAL-011.whatItIs: This checks whether sensitive information — a typed password, a PIN being entered, customer data on a screen, a visible access code — can be casually seen by someone standing nearby, with zero technical effort involved, just because of how a desk or counter is arranged, or a habit like saying a PIN out loud.
SOCIAL-011.rootCause: Open-plan offices, shared desks, and customer service counters are designed for collaboration and efficient use of space, not visual privacy — so screens, keypads, and paperwork often end up facing hallways, shared tables, or customers, simply because no one deliberately checked what's visible from those angles.
SOCIAL-011.impact: An observed credential or PIN can be used directly and immediately, with no technical exploitation step required at all, and observed customer or employee PII displayed on an unshielded screen can constitute a reportable data-exposure incident on its own even without any further action by the observer.
stepsToIdentify: Map high-risk sightlines in open work areas — desks facing walkways, monitors visible from shared meeting rooms, reception-area screens visible to waiting visitors.
Observe login and PIN-entry behavior (badge PIN pads, POS terminals, workstation unlock) for any pattern of unshielded entry or verbal recitation of a code.
Note whether privacy screens (physical filters) are deployed at any high-risk desks, and whether their absence correlates with roles handling more sensitive data (finance, HR, customer support).
Check common areas (cafes, elevators, shared transit) near the facility for employees visibly working on sensitive material where the public could observe.
Assess printed-document handling at shared desks or printer stations for documents left face-up or unretrieved for extended periods.
Cross-reference any observed information (a partial password pattern, a customer record) against the OSINT dossier to assess whether it adds meaningfully new exposure.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the SOW's authorized observation locations and whether photographic evidence of screens/keypads is permitted.
Conduct discreet, passive observation during normal business activity without engaging or distracting employees in a way that could itself compromise safety or normal operations.
Record specific instances of exposure (what was visible, from what distance/angle, for how long) rather than a vague general impression.
Where photographic evidence is authorized, capture only what's needed to substantiate the finding, avoiding capture of unrelated personal or unrelated third-party information beyond what's necessary.
Note any instance where a customer or visitor (rather than the tester) would have had the same sightline, since this indicates the exposure isn't limited to a controlled test scenario.
Classify findings by realistic sensitivity (a visible internal memo vs. a visible customer SSN) for the report rather than a flat count of observations.

variants: Customer-facing service-counter variant assessing whether customer PII on an agent's screen is visible to the next person in line.
Remote/public-workspace variant assessing employees working in cafes, airports, or shared co-working spaces on client-visible material.
Verbal-disclosure variant assessing whether sensitive information (account numbers, PINs) is spoken aloud within earshot of others in open areas or over the phone in a shared space.

Executive-area variant assessing whether higher floors/executive offices, often assumed to be lower-risk due to restricted access, still have unshielded sightlines from shared corridors or glass-walled offices.
mitigation: Deploy physical privacy screens on monitors at desks with walkway-facing or shared-space sightlines, prioritized by role sensitivity (finance, HR, customer support, executive assistants).
Reposition high-risk workstations (customer service counters, badge/PIN entry points) away from public or shared-space sightlines where feasible.
Train staff on PIN/password entry hygiene — shielding the keypad, avoiding verbal recitation of codes — as a specific, concrete behavior rather than generic 'be aware of your surroundings' guidance.
Enforce a clean-desk policy with periodic spot checks for sensitive printed material left unattended at shared desks or printer stations.
Extend awareness training to cover remote/public workspace behavior (cafes, transit, co-working spaces) for staff who regularly work outside the office.
Apply automatic screen-lock timeouts aggressively at high-risk desks so a brief unattended moment doesn't compound a shoulder-surfing exposure into an unattended, unlocked session.
Review customer-facing counter layout specifically, since PII exposure to the next customer in line carries direct regulatory/privacy-notification implications distinct from an internal-only finding.

SOCIAL-012.prerequisites: Written authorization explicitly covering physical media drop testing, the specific 'payload' behavior authorized (a benign beacon-only callback vs. anything further), and confirmation the drives will only ever phone home to an assessor-controlled endpoint. Blank/prepared USB drives (or a BadUSB-style HID-emulating device for the more advanced variant) and, for the beacon variant, a controlled listening endpoint to log check-ins.
SOCIAL-012.whatItIs: A USB drop attack leaves branded, official-looking USB drives somewhere employees pass by often — a parking lot, the lobby, a break room — betting that curiosity ('what's on this?') or a helpful instinct ('I should figure out whose this is') gets someone to plug it into a work computer. Depending on the setup, that might trigger an autorun-style payload, or a more modern variant where the drive pretends to be a keyboard and types out commands. In this test, the payload is harmless and just logs that it ran.
SOCIAL-012.rootCause: Company computers often still allow unmanaged USB drives to be plugged in and read (or even autorun content) with no restriction, and there's usually no policy or training addressing the very well-documented human habit of picking up a found USB drive and plugging it in out of curiosity or a sense of duty to return it.
SOCIAL-012.impact: A real malicious drop can deliver anything from a simple beacon (confirming the target is compromisable) to a full initial-access foothold or credential harvester, entirely bypassing network-perimeter and email-security controls since the delivery mechanism is physical rather than digital.
stepsToIdentify: Review endpoint configuration for autorun/autoplay behavior on removable media across a representative sample of workstations.
Assess whether USB port control or an allow-listing solution (Microsoft Defender ASR removable-media rules, an endpoint DLP agent) is deployed and enforced.
Check whether the organization has any policy or training addressing found/unknown USB media specifically, distinct from general phishing awareness.
Identify realistic drop locations (parking areas, lobby, elevator lobby, break room) consistent with where employees would plausibly find and pick up an item.

Confirm whether security operations has visibility to detect an unexpected new USB mass-storage or HID device event on an endpoint, which would matter regardless of whether this specific test succeeds.
Establish the specific, benign payload behavior to be used (a beacon-only callback, a marker file, or a simulated HID keystroke sequence typing a benign message) before any drive is prepared.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the SOW's authorized drop locations, the specific benign payload behavior, and the takedown/collection time for any un-retrieved drives.

Prepare the drives with only the pre-agreed benign payload (a beacon callback to an assessor-controlled endpoint, or a marker file with no further action) and verify in a lab environment that the payload does exactly what's authorized and nothing more.
Place drives in the authorized locations, using plausible but non-deceptive branding (a generic label, not impersonating a specific real employee or executive by name).
Monitor the controlled endpoint for check-ins, logging timestamp and originating network context only, without collecting any further data from the connecting machine.
Retrieve or account for all un-triggered drives at the agreed end time, since an un-retrieved physical drive left in place indefinitely is itself a residual risk to manage.

Where a check-in is received, do not proceed beyond the pre-agreed benign action even if further access appears technically possible — report the successful connection as the finding, not as a jumping-off point for deeper access.

examplePayloads.command: echo 'This drive is part of an authorized security assessment. If found, please contact security@target-company.com.' > README.txt   # placed alongside the beacon payload so a curious non-victim can identify the test immediately

examplePayloads.command: curl -s 'https://assessor-controlled-endpoint.test/beacon?drive_id=lot-a-03' >/dev/null 2>&1

examplePayloads.label: Assessor-controlled listener for beacon check-ins
examplePayloads.command: python3 -m http.server 8080   # bound to the assessor's controlled endpoint only, logging incoming beacon requests

examplePayloads.label: Drop-location log entry (documentation, not a tool)
examplePayloads.command: Record: drive ID, location, placement timestamp, retrieval/expiry timestamp.

examplePayloads.label: HID-emulation variant bench verification (lab only, not deployed without separate explicit authorization)
examplePayloads.command: Verify a BadUSB-style device only types the pre-agreed benign confirmation string when tested on the assessor's own lab machine before any consideration of field use.

examplePayloads.label: Post-engagement drive accounting
examplePayloads.command: Confirm all prepared drive IDs are either retrieved, triggered-and-logged, or explicitly written off in the report as un-recovered at engagement close.

variants: HID-emulating (BadUSB-style) variant where the device presents as a keyboard and types a benign, logged command rather than relying on autorun of stored files.
Branded/context-specific variant using packaging consistent with a plausible source (a conference giveaway, a courier envelope) rather than a plain unlabeled drive.
Charging-cable variant (a modified cable rather than a drive) testing the same curiosity-driven behavior via a different physical form factor.
Mail-delivered variant testing whether a USB drive arriving by internal mail with a plausible cover letter is treated differently from one found in a parking lot.
mitigation: Disable autorun/autoplay for removable media at the endpoint policy level across the fleet.
Deploy USB device control (allow-listing known, organization-issued media; blocking or alerting on unknown mass-storage and HID devices) via endpoint protection or a dedicated DLP agent.
Train staff explicitly on found-media handling: hand it to security/IT rather than plugging it into any work (or personal) device.
Provide a simple, low-friction reporting path for found media, mirroring the phishing-report button's ease of use.
Ensure security operations has alerting for unexpected new removable-storage or HID-device events on managed endpoints, independent of this specific test.
Periodically repeat this assessment, since susceptibility often changes meaningfully after the first awareness campaign addressing it specifically.

Extend the same media-control policy to any air-gapped or industrial-control environments in scope, where removable media is often a primary infection vector precisely because network-based defenses don't apply.

SOCIAL-013.prerequisites: Written authorization to observe unattended workstations in open areas and, where explicitly permitted, to briefly approach an unlocked, unattended machine to confirm the session is genuinely active (without entering credentials, opening files, or taking any action beyond confirming the lock state). No special tooling required beyond observation and timing.
SOCIAL-013.whatItIs: This checks whether the company's screen-lock timeout is actually enforced by policy — and, just as importantly, whether people actually respect it. If an employee steps away from their desk, does the machine sit unlocked and exposed to anyone walking by until the timeout kicks in? Or does it never lock at all because someone's turned that setting off?
SOCIAL-013.rootCause: An already-unlocked session has no further login check standing between a random passerby and everything on that screen. If the timeout is set too long, applied inconsistently across different device types, or routinely disabled by employees for convenience, the control looks fine on paper but doesn't actually protect anything in practice.
SOCIAL-013.impact: A walk-up attacker with access to an unlocked session inherits the full access of the logged-in user instantly — email, file shares, internal systems — with no exploitation effort required at all, and because no credential was used, the activity may not appear anomalous to monitoring that specifically watches for unusual authentication events.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the organization's configured group policy or MDM setting for screen-lock inactivity timeout, and compare it against the value actually observed on a sample of real workstations.
Observe open work areas during natural break periods (lunch, coffee runs, meetings) for unattended, unlocked screens rather than relying on policy documentation alone.
Check whether the timeout is applied consistently across device types (desktop, laptop, kiosk/shared terminal) or whether some categories are exempted or misconfigured.
Assess whether employees have a habit of manually locking (Windows+L / Control+Command+Q) when stepping away briefly, independent of the automatic timeout.
Review whether shared or kiosk-style terminals (reception desks, shared lab machines) have an appropriately shorter timeout given their higher walk-up exposure.

Identify any process or technical exception (a long-running batch job, a presentation display) that legitimately requires a longer timeout, so the finding can distinguish a genuine business exception from an unmanaged gap.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the SOW's authorization to observe and, if permitted, briefly approach an unattended unlocked workstation solely to confirm and time the lock state — not to interact with any application or data.
During normal business activity, observe unattended workstations and record the elapsed time from the employee stepping away to either a manual lock, an automatic lock, or continued exposure.

Where approach is authorized, confirm the session is genuinely active (rather than already locked and merely appearing active from a distance) without touching the keyboard/mouse beyond what's needed to observe the lock indicator.
Do not open any application, file, or browser tab, and do not move the mouse in a way that could be mistaken for actual use of the session.
If the employee returns during observation, disengage naturally without drawing attention, consistent with a passive-observation methodology.

Record the specific device/location pattern (desk type, department, device category) rather than only an aggregate exposure count, since remediation is often device-type-specific (e.g. kiosk terminals need a shorter timeout than the general fleet).
